title: The Mountain Where Elders Were Left
text:
A Japanese folk tale tells of a province ruled by a harsh lord, where food was so scarce that the old were said to be carried into the mountains and left there to die once they could no longer work.

A poor farmer's mother reached that age. With a heavy heart he lifted her onto his back and climbed into the mountains. As they went deeper into the forest, he noticed that his mother was reaching out and breaking off small twigs from the branches they passed, dropping them along the path.

He thought she meant to find her way back. But when they reached the place where he had to leave her, she told him why she had done it. The path was steep and confusing, she said, and she did not want her son to lose his way going home in the dark. She had marked the trail for him.

The son was overcome. Even as he was abandoning her, her only thought was for his safety. He could not leave her. He carried her back down the mountain in the night and hid her at home, caring for her in secret. In some tellings her wisdom later helped him solve impossible riddles set by the lord, who then abolished the cruel custom.
lesson: A parent's love does not stop to calculate what it gets back. Remembering what our parents gave us can change how we treat them when they become a burden.
source: Japanese folktale (Ubasute or Obasute legend); early versions of the abandonment theme in the Yamato Monogatari and Konjaku Monogatari
caveat: Ubasute is a legend; there is no firm historical evidence that it was ever a common practice.
